posts.body_html:
I messed up Bogman. I went to my favorite Japanese restaurant, got into a very intriguing conversation with the chef, and totally missed the opportunity to break out a fat chunk of wasabi to sample with my lunch! Probably would have helped if I brought some in the first place, but if I had it in my pocket at that momement, I would have taken on your double dog dare!!!! I think I'm going to hook him up some really good quality, home made hoshigaki and wasabi for X-mas, and see if that can't loosen him up to the idea of me bringing in outside food LOL!!!!

Some new pics, taken 11/16/18. I'm sooo hooked on Wasabi, probably would need rehab to get off of it! With cold days and cold nights, these plants are starting to grow very fast again:





Somewhat decent example of how these "stems" can be construed as rhizomes. This just recaps. the cloudiness of using such a term to describe the wasabi stem (edit: LOL these guys say it's a rhizome: )





Established division with an already nice start to the stem! I bet by spring, this will have enough to harvest, but I like to grow my stems big before harvesting:

posts.body_html:
Dayum, home made hoshigaki too!? What persimmons are you using? Can't keep D. kaki here, just a tad too cold. I even tried Nikita's Gift, the kaki x virginiana  cross, but it croaked, too; might have been all the rain. It's still raining here like mad.

I'm hoping to graft some superior virginiana twigs onto seedlings. When I was in college, I'd often walk 2-3 miles to the Univ., especially after my VW blew a valve and I was rebuilding/hot rodding it in my basement. On the way, I came across a tree which produced flavorful, firm, non-astrigent fruits; no need to wait for late Oct.-Dec. They were amazing, and wild, growing 30 feet from the road. One day, I walked home to find the county widened route 123 and destroyed it, along with a colony of Isotria orchids.

Now, there's  good persimmon growing under a power line, near the nursery; it keeps getting hacked to the ground by the maintenance crew. So far, it resprouts. I need to start a bunch of virginiana seedlings and go tree sampling. As you'd guess by the "virginiana", there are a lot around here. Some are friggin' nasty astringent, others very good, with strong apricot-like flavors.

Keep that Wasabi jones going! Let me know when you have a surplus and want to sell some rhizome/stem… "stemzome"? . I want to try the freeze-dry method, for long term storage and convenience. Mine are growing slowly, since it's hard to keep them cool enough.

mmm… mashed potatoes w/ wasabi, edamame w/ wasabi, shrimp w/ wasabi, wasabi vinaigrette  ..drool...

Diospyros lotus is less tolerant of wet soils compared to D. virginiana, I wonder if your Nitka's gift was on lotus or on D. kaki, that could have been the issue. In California, D. virginia seedlings wilt once the soil gets dry, they want lots of moisture. D. lotus will rot if given the same amount of water.


Ironically, most persimmon varieties first entered the US via California, yet it's near impossible to get any other varieties here other than Hachiya and Fuyu (California has a strict quarantine on Persimmon trees). The hoshigaki comes from Hachiya, and FINALLY!!! I have one that's starting to form the white sugar crystals on the outside. It took about 5 weeks before the first signs of crystal formation. Quality of the final product is much better with fruit that were left on the tree for as long as possible. In california, you can let the ripe fruit hang long after the leaves have all fallen off the tree.


Okay, back to Wasabi. For sure, I'm going to grow a lot of these out and will offer some to eat hopefully by fall 2019. I tried both Daruma and Mazuma, but I lack culinary experience to know which one is better. To me, both are outstanding, except Mazuma seems more productive here. Judging taste is like carrying a boom-box on your shoulder versus installing a surround sound system in your car: you don't know how good it really can be until you have experienced the best.

posts.body_html:
According to the vendor, the Nikita's Gift was grafted onto D. virginiana root stocks. I was surprised that there weren't even suckers coming up; that's why I suspect rot. Persimmons are late to leaf out here. It started raining like crazy in late May and continued until a couple weeks ago. We had a few sunny days, but the soil was always soaked. Great for fungus, bad for fruiting plants.

There is a myth that the native persimmons need to be picked after frost, that freezing improves them. That has been proven false. What matters is the same as what you are indicating: the longer the fruit sits on the tree, the better it will be, with certain provisos. One year, we had unusually late frosts; first frost was in Nov. The persimmons were outstanding before that, maturing on the tree well ahead of freezes. An early, very hard freeze can stop maturation and negatively effect ripening/quality. Beyond any of this, some fruits are genetically producing less astringent fruit. We have many out here that are awful, no matter how long they're on the tree. Opossum and Raccoon are the primary seed dispersion vectors, and they aren't too picky about what they eat!

2019 isn't that far away. Since you'll have an "assembly line" of plants, every year could be a harvest year; lucky you! Sign me up for the excess/for-sale harvest. If the freeze-dry thing works, I'll send you some, sealed in Mylar with oxygen absorbing packets (non toxic iron based). I'm thinking, if the stem is split lengthwise in halves or thirds (1/2 inch- 5/8 inch is optimal for freeze drying), minimal chemical mixing will take place. Once completely dry, the stems can be powdered without reacting. Might have to tinker with the machines settings, for best results.

posts.body_html:
Some new pics! Okay, to recap, I have 2 varieties, daruma and mazuma (since it's near impossible to acquire any other varieties here in california). Here's Daruma, which grows like a weed whenever it's cold outside:




I won't lie though, I prefer Mazuma, at least in my climate. It seems to be more productive here. This is an established division that is literally getting packed up for shipping, check out the size of the rhizome on it! These plants, if grown well, can be harvested by next winter. The large size of the rhizome, as well as the health of the plant you begin with makes all the difference in the world. It took me I think close to 2 years before I could have my first taste of wasabi:


You could technically harvest the plant at this stage, but it seems to be more practical to grow it out:

posts.body_html:
some updated pics of Wasabia japnonica 'Mazuma.' These are grown outdoors, but are kept by the house, so they're slightly protected. They all froze two nights ago: the leaves wilted and I didn't think they'd make it, but hours later, you couldn't tell they froze! It was 24F that morning, but I think these plants were exposed to maybe 29F. I've since started to cover them because they seem only slightly freeze tolerant.

On a different note, in the past, when I tried mazuma, it was sweet and flavorful, but not overly spicy. Around December of last year, I grated some up and put a huge chunk on my sashimi, which was a huge mistake! It was so powerful I could barely breath! Fortunately, like horse radish, it's powerful for only a few seconds and then it mellows out. I harvested the rhizome when it hadn't put on much growth and had stayed practically dormant all summer long since it's too hot here for good summer growth. I think the rhizomes are significantly more powerful when growing slowly like that compared to when they're putting on massive growth like now.


Pics taken 2/23/22:


smaller divisions went into a community pot:


bigger divisions were potted separately. This one is already technically harvestable, but I'm growing it out instead:


A rooted cutting, about 2 weeks after being divided:



notice these plants are getting direct sunlight: if the temperatures are between 33 to about 59F, they can handle full sun. Anything warmer and the leaves will start to wilt:

posts.body_html:
some updated pics of the Wasabi collection. The plants are looking surprisingly well this time of year, despite being exposed to several heat waves. I think the key is that they're now under shade cloth all day long (I took it off for the pics), which makes a huge difference. Last summer, I merely put them in the shade, but they got morning sun once the fall approached, since the sun moved it's position relative to the grow area. Morning sun is great during the winter when day temperatures are in the mid 60's at most, but it stresses them out really bad if the air temperatures are 70F or above.

Pics taken June 4, 2022:




Some new acquisitions hardening off outdoors. Despite having years of experience growing Wasabi, I almost killed these, they're so dang hard to acclimate, they must have been grown in a greenhouse or under lights because hours after planting them, they wilted, even in pure shade! It took a lot to get these to eventually start producing new leaves and every last one of them so far survived:

posts.body_html:
After a very rough grow season last year, the wasabi plants are finally looking prime again! About 3 months ago, you couldn't recognize these plants, they looked SOOO bad...worse than ever before! That was probably a combination of a prolonged heat wave last fall coupled with just too much light and temperatures being too high for too long. The plants went dormant and produce little to no growth from around May thru November.

Just when it cooled down enough, the plants got rained on and sat in trays of water, which was no good, so that further set them back! Without the trays, they would dry up too fast during the summer, and I totally forgot to remove them because it's been a long time since we had serious rain. This past winter, we had record breaking precipitation! They were kept under 70% shade cloth because some days it was sunny, and other days it was cloudy. During the rainy season, it was cloudy most of the time, and the plants didn't like near freezing, dark conditions so they sulked a bit.

Fast forward to now, I cleaned up all the dead leaves, added some fresh top soil to all the pots, and gave them a good dose of organic tomato fertilizer, and gave them direct sunlight from sun up till about noon, and it has made all the difference in the world! Pics taken 2/23/23:

wasabia japonica 'Mazuma,' very reliable cultivar that I've had multiple harvests from now:


Wasabia japonica Mazuma flowers and fertilized ovary:


finally. FINALLY! Wasabia japonica 'Misho' starting to put on some good looking growth. this is a new cultivar that I acquired last summer, which in retrospect was a very bad time to acclimate right out of tissue culture! It's hard to harden them off from such delicate conditions in the first place, but compound that with hot temperatures and it's super difficult. There is one clone in this picture that has purple stems (petioles), while the rest don't! No idea if that's genetic or environmental:


After nearly 7 years of having this clone, it's still alive and just starting to thrive again. Wasabia japonica 'Daruma':


Another picture of Daruma, such beautiful leaves:


Hard to beat the growth and productivity of Mazuma:


The biggest challenge right now is managing slugs, no matter how many you get rid of, more come back!


Some small back up divisions of Misho, made as many as I could just in case something happened to the mother plants:

posts.body_html:
The wasabi plants CRASHED HARD last summer/fall when it got hot here! They looked so bad and I was SOOOO bent out of shape! What ends up happening is the growth point completely stops pushing out new growth and the plants appear to go dormant, and during this process they look absolutely horrible! BUT.....after many months of being cool, they were moved into full sun during the winter when air temperatures were no warmer than in the low 50's and then they starting growing strong, so even though they were neglected and not repotted in time, I eventually got to them and now they're in optimus PRIME shape BABY! Oh ya!

One thing I figured out: one layer of 70% shade cloth isn't enough, especially with warm air temperatures! I ran out of shade cloth so I put a layer of frost cloth on top of the shade cloth, and so far that's working but when we get into hot fall temperatures, I think 2 layers of 70% shade cloth will do the trick! Keep in mind, this is a spot that gets sun from about 7am to 11am, with the rest of the day pure shade!

Anyways, some updated pics! Here's a unique clone of Wasabia japonica 'Misho' that has purple stems! all of the other misho clones have white stems! Misho is turning out to be a winner: it grows strong just like Mazuma except the rhizome and leaves, IMO, are better looking:


Close up of the purple stemmed Misho clone. Sorry, don't have pics of the rhizome just yet, I got a glimpse of it when transplanting them:


Mazuma back to it's robust self! Quite a relief to finally nurse them back to health after so many months of seeing massive decline and just absolute nasty dead leaves. I'm realizing I should take pics next time it happens, although as eminem once rapped, hopefully "next time there will be no next time":



This picture was taken at the crack of dawn! Remember, these plants are growing under shade cloth, I had to lift it off to take pictures. With direct sun like this, even early in the morning, those leaves will start to wilt in 5-10 minutes, that's how sensitive they are!
